newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices jump as Europe starts 1997 in freezer.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices jump as Europe starts 1997 in freezer.

text.p: Oil prices began 1997 with a rally as freezing weather gripped much of Europe, stoking demand for winter heating oil and memories of a similar cold snap in the United States a year ago.

The February futures contract for international benchmark Brent crude oil on London's International Petroleum Exchange was up 56 cents a barrel at $24.37 by 1030 GMT on Thursday from its closing price of 1996.

Brent prices are still around 70 cents below a six-year high of $25.06 a barrel hit a few months ago but traders said an extended cold spell combined with low oil storage tanks might trigger a fresh assault on that peak.
"We see oil prices being volatile in the short term but with an upward bias," said Alan Haywood of Bankers Trust International oil division in London.
"It's hard to be bearish with the cold weather but the market has been jumpy over the holiday period and will take a few days to settle down," he said.
Severe cold weather continued across much of Europe on Thursday and energy demand is expected to be well above normal, according to private forecasters Weather Services Corporation.
Some waterways which take heating oil up the river Rhine to the important German market were partially blocked by ice early on Thursday and likely to cause delays, traders said.

Germany, easily Europe's biggest heating oil consumer, has been running on unusually thin inventories. German household stocks of heating oil fell in November to about 62 percent of capacity from 68 percent last year, traders estimate.

Gas oil (heating oil) futures traded in London have gained some six percent over the past month and January futures were up $7.50 a tonne at $231.25 in mid-morning. But for German consumers a barge of oil loading prompt in Rotterdam costs $2 a tonne above futures even before transport costs are added.
"It's gas oil-driven" said Scott Carter, senior oil trader at Tosco UK Ltd in London.
He said the premium paid for gas oil above Brent crude had risen 50 cents a barrel to $6.50 since Tuesday.
Adding a bullish twist to the Europe was news earlier this week that China needs to import about one million tonnes of diesel fuel over the next month to ease a domestic shortage.
Diesel fuel comes from the same cut of an oil barrel as heating oil and the Chinese demand might suck some of that oil out of Europe.

Meanwhile, in the key northeastern United States, distillate stocks -- which include heating oil -- are 13 percent lower than year-ago levels. The latest stocks figures for the United States are due to be released later on Thursday.
Oil traders have been sensitised to the impact of freezing weather in recent years after blizzards swept the northeastern United States a year ago.
That cold snap sent oil prices soaring before talk last spring of a deal to allow Iraq to resume selling oil for the first time since the Gulf War pushed them lower again.
Despite the United Nations oil-for-food deal, finally implemented on December 17, the average price of a barrel of Brent over 1996 of $20.32 was around 20 percent higher than in 1995.
Oil markets have found little difficulty so far in absorbing the limited volumes of Iraqi oil exports permitted under the oil-for-food exchange.

Iraq started exports earlier this month under one of 21 contracts for some 500,000 barrels a day of crude sales, enough at current prices to raise the $2 billion that it is allowed over a six-month period to pay for humanitarian needs.
